utterances.text: I can find that reference and provide it through Ms. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would please do so. The previous one, by the way, if it is page 1 and 2 and we find in the transcript it's page 1, then it's not too difficult for those following the proceedings that after 1, 2 follows. utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's not a correction to the transcript. In fact, it's just I'd like to offer that in. Mr. Ivetic had initially wondered about the description in e-court to that video. Okay. So we've got the transcript page 11536.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, 11536, that's still the 24th of May. I'm with you on that page. We have 14 -- let me see. Could you take us to a line -- because I see at the end of 536 I see a reference to P1482.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. It was offered into evidence at transcript page 11535, at line 10, and then the discussion continues, as I understand, to 11536. It doesn't relate to the transcript itself. In fact, there is nothing incorrect in the transcript. It's simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it was marked for identification after Mr. Ivetic. I'm just wondering -- are there still any objections, Mr. Lukic, or would you like to consult Mr. Ivetic on the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would rather consult with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then hear from you in the course of this day or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not later than by tomorrow. Ms. Hasan, anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No, that's everything. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hasan. Then if there is nothing else, Mr. Shin, at least you're behind the lectern so I suppose that it will be you. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness, which I do understand is Mr. Pepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution is ready for its next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. I do understand that Mr. Pepic is accompanied by counsel, and I take it mainly for any matter related to Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honours, and I take it then we won't need to remind -- the issue of providing the Rule 90(E) caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that we will verify with counsel whether he has discussed the matter with his client.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pepic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. Could I invite to you make that solemn declaration? Mr. Usher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pepic. Please be seated. Mr. Pepic, you're assisted by Mr. Petrovic as counsel. He's not there to be consulted for answers to questions. He's there in order to intervene, if need be, if there is a risk that by answering a question truthfully that you would incriminate yourself and how to proceed on from that moment. Has he explained to you the Rule, the relevant Rule, which is Rule 90(E)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can proceed. You'll first be examined by Mr. Shin. Mr. Shin is counsel for the Prosecution and you'll find him to your right. Mr. Shin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, and just before we begin, I'll just briefly introduce my learned friend, Mr. Vladimir Petrovic, who may be known to Your Honours. And Mr. Petrovic had indicated that he may wish to raise some preliminary matters, so I will give -- pass the mic to him right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, if there is any matter you want to raise, you first have to consider whether it is appropriate to do it in the presence of Mr. Pepic because any guidance which might be -- might be -- might be understood to be in the matter you want to raise is inappropriate. So please tell me whether you think you can raise the matter in the presence of your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that I can, since it's just a question of a few principled matters. If you permit me, Mr. Shin informed me that he intends to tender two documents under 92 ter to the Trial Chamber, that is the witness statement provided to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities in 2000 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the year, and could Mr. Petrovic please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you slow down and tell us again what year that statement was taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I will try. The statement provided to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities is from 2005. And the second document that the Prosecutor intends to tender under 92 ter, as I have been informed, is the record from a previous case before this Tribunal, from the 9th of July, 2007. Both the documents contain some parts which, in my opinion, can be self-incriminating to the witness. Since he's here going to confirm and accept these two documents as his own, and these two documents would then become an integral part of his testimony and will corroborate any of his oral testimony here, it seems to me that some parts of these two documents would need to be omitted as part of the 92 ter bundle. Your Honours, I can inform you which parts of the two documents are the ones which in my opinion are potentially self-incriminating to the witness and, therefore, I believe are not suitable to be included in the 92 ter bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, first of all, Mr. Shin is on his feet. The question for me arises what is the appropriate remedy if an answer, including part of a statement, would be potentially incriminating, what the rules say about that. Mr. Shin? But before further dealing with that matter, Mr. Shin?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Mr. President. You're anticipating exactly part of the points that I wish to make. I would also point out that the prior testimony from the Popovic case was in open session, so it was already a matter of the public record, so I'm not sure what further issues may arise from trying to -- my learned friend said omitted, but let's say there may be some other approach that would be a solution, if necessary. Now, the areas of the SIPA statement are also identical in substance to these areas in the Popovic testimony that was in open session so I just wanted to note that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there are two issues, Mr. Petrovic. The first one being that what is tendered by the Prosecution is already in the public domain and confirming it now would not add that much to what is already there. Second, what is the appropriate remedy if an answer to a question is potentially incriminating. Could you please address both matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. As for the first issue, both statements were provided by the witness. It's correct that the one statement was provided in public session, but both statements were given without the presence of his Defence attorney. At the time when he provided both statements nobody was there to advise him that what he was saying could possibly be self-incriminating. Therefore, even though it was provided publicly, this is the situation in which he sought legal advice, he sought a legal adviser, he wanted somebody to take care of that on his behalf, and that situation is different from this situation which was there previously. So it is no longer a question of whether he -- it's not a question of whether this happened in public or in private session. The essence is whether he had a legal adviser presence or not. He answered without receiving advice from anyone that he should not do that. And in that situation, I believe that this Trial Chamber should do everything to protect this witness from being exposed to a situation which could be potentially self-incriminating. As for your second question, according to Rule 90(E) of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, he has the right not to answer questions which could potentially be self-incriminating. By ruling out these parts from these statements, in that way that would be not answering questions which in his view could be self-incriminating. Of course, the Trial Chamber could seek that the witness answers those questions, but then we would have the situation when that answer, possible answer, could not be used in any subsequent proceedings against him. So his position is that he does not wish to talk about those matters. Of course, if the Trial Chamber considers that he should speak of them, then he will, but only on the basis of the decision of the Trial Chamber on the basis of Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're taking a different passion now as you did before. You said they should be stricken. First of all, Rule 90(E) does not give a right not to answer any question. Rule 90(E) gives a witness the right to object to answering a question on which the Chamber then will decide. We do understand that such an objection is made in relation to some portions of the statement. Could you please identify which portions they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honours. As for the transcript of the 9th of July, 2007, pages 13556, lines 15 to 25; page 13559, line 12, to page 13560, line 15; page 13566, lines 21 to 23; page 13567, lines 10 to 15; page 13580, lines 17 to 24; page 13594, lines 14 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're going at such a pace that I can't follow it. I am now at 13567, you said 10 to 15. Next one, 580, 17 to 24. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the transcript. I took it that you had some objections against portions of the record of the interview. Please proceed with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the transcript, there are just three more references. And they are 13594, lines 14 to 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not in my copy which makes me believe that it might not be part of the tendered transcripts but I have to verify that. Mr. Shin, could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. President, that that would not be the position of the transcript that we would tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For me it stops at 580. Is that -- no, let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, yes, Your Honour, you're correct, it's the last page would be 13580.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so therefore, that is moot, Mr. Petrovic. We now move to the record of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have the B/C/S version of the document. Unfortunately, I don't have the English version. I believe that my learned friend Mr. Shin could assist there. In B/C/S, this is paragraph 9 on page 4, and also the first full paragraph on page 5. I did not receive, unfortunately, the English version and I had no way of obtaining one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you asked for it? Have you asked, Mr. Shin, if only this morning, for the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not ask for it, Your Honour, no, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: More or less the problem is now ours instead of yours. That's not what we expect. Mr. Shin, could you assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if I may assist, the -- if -- if my learned friend is referring to page 4, paragraph 9, of the B/C/S, that would be, I believe, a paragraph beginning "tada je meni"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In English that would then be on page 8 and that would be paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see, page 8, paragraph 4, starts with, "At least Oficir," in English, and I see the same word in the B/C/S version on page 4, 9th paragraph, yes. So we start from that one, Mr. Petrovic, and then you wanted -- yes, "Oficir then told me." Where does it stop, the portion, or does the whole paragraph -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just that paragraph, Your Honour, and on page 5 of the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. That's the paragraph which ends with the last line, "This stoppage of traffic lasted for about one hour."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Next would be what, page 5 in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, if I may, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you just leave me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First full paragraph, page 5, again starts in the B/C/S with the word "Oficir," and, Mr. Shin, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- by any chance the second paragraph of page 10?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: It would be page 9, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And it would be the first full paragraph which actually appears in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me see. Okay, "With his arm in bandages, Oficir returned ...," that's how it starts. And it ends with, "Our detachment was assembled or fully assembled in Sandici." Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is hereby clearly on the record. Mr. Shin, forgive me for not having every detail in my memory. Was the witness reminded of Rule 90(E) when he gave his testimony in Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, in our motion for counsel on behalf of the witness we had indicated that he was. I would just note briefly we do have an English version of the BiH statement for my learned friend, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Petrovic, if a witness has been informed about Rule 90(E), if he then nevertheless answers the questions, do you think that we should then exclude that in the future where every single part of the Rule has been followed? Is the appropriate remedy then to later on say he wasn't advised? He was advised by the Chamber, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Chamber did remind him, but in my view, regardless of the caution, this is an individual who isn't a lawyer and who maybe hasn't grasped how far this caution reaches and what its significance is and that's why we should proceed the way I suggested. I am not sure that the scope of what is covered by the caution is adequate enough in the case of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then my next question would be, if we would now tell the witness or now say that he is forced to answer the question, would that have any effect on any prosecuting authority to use, then, the Popovic testimony rather than this one? Because even if his words today cannot be held against him, then still the words in Popovic could, if -- unless I'm mistaken. If you have any comment on that, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's correct. However, he can say that at the time he did not have counsel who would be able to give him legal advice, and that could make his position less grave, although it may not rule out the possibility of a criminal procedure initiated against him, but he would have arguments militating against that. So --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Petrovic repeat what he said last?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what you said last because the interpreters did not catch it. What is on the record is, "... but he would have arguments militating against that," and could you resume from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He would have arguments against it, but he could not rule out the possibility that such a document may be used so I agree with you on that score. But he could provide arguments as to the circumstances leading to that situation, and that could make his situation easier and much more favourable, should he be confronted with such a situation. That's my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question: Is there any concrete reason which would lead you to believe that any prosecution is prepared at this moment against the witness? Or is he charged anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, based on what the witness told me, he is being treated as a suspect. He cannot tell precisely in which case and concerning which circumstances, but he believes that his status is that of a suspect and that he has been treated as such on a number of occasions before the BH court. As far as I know there is no indictment that has been issued or any other formal document against him but that's the status that he currently holds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when was that, that he last -- he felt for the first time to be treated as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact date, but it was after giving evidence in both these instances that were the subject of our discussion today. Now, as to when this happened, the witness may assist us. At any rate it was after his testimony in the Popovic case and after he had given this statement to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is close to eight years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would prefer not to guess. Perhaps the witness should tell us when exactly this was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a date for the statement, isn't it? That's 2005, October, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He acquired that status at some point after that point in time. When that was exactly is something that the witness can tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us under what circumstances and how you learned that you were a suspect before the BiH authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received a summons, perhaps a year ago, from the Prosecution of the BH court to testify in the indictment against Jevic et al. I was told in that summons that I should have a legal representative with me since I was a suspect. It may have been a year or a year and a half ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Simply, Your Honours, to note that that doesn't change the fact that the earlier materials are in open session, when he had been provided the Rule 930(E) caution, and in addition, the remedies point, Your Honours have already pointed out certainly striking or omitting is not among those, for the purposes of Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Give me one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I'll give you the Chamber's ruling on the objection you made. You have -- on behalf of Mr. Pepic, you have objected to making the statement on the relevant portions which, as you say, may tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber accepts that this objection is made. The Chamber compels the witness to answer the questions; that means that those portions of the statement are included in any statement or transcript which we may admit. Testimony compelled in this way shall not, as the rules say, be used as evidence in a subsequent Prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony. That applies in relation to the testimony the witness gives today. The Chamber has no jurisdiction, nor any other competence, to rule on the use of any statement or any testimony made previously in another case or before another authority. Is this ruling clear to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, those portions will not be stricken. The Chamber has considered whether we should make them confidential in order to give further protection to the witness. The Chamber has decided not to make those portions confidential, since they are on the public record already. Then I think we can proceed. Witness, it may be a bit complex for you what we discussed, I don't know whether you have fully understood it, otherwise I'll try to explain it in a few words. Whatever you say today, even if you repeat something you said earlier, we insist on you giving those answers, and what you say today, including references to what you said earlier, cannot be used against you in any other proceedings. But the Chamber is not in a position to say that what you said in the Popovic case or what you said anywhere else, that that cannot be used against you in any future proceedings. That is just beyond our competence. So we focus exclusively on what you say today, including the portions where you repeat what you said earlier. That's, I hope, an understandable explanation for you, as far as your situation is concerned. Is it clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Pepic, a proper good morning to you. Could you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Milenko Pepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, we have been discussing this but, for the record, is it correct that you provided a statement to the BiH state investigation and protection agency in the Ministry of Security and the statement was dated 26 October 2005?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. I may be referring to this document as the SIPA statement, SIPA being the acronym in English for this Bosnian state entity, and as I understand it, actually, the English acronym is used in Bosnia. Now, my next question: For the purposes of that SIPA statement you were informed of your obligation to tell the truth and of the consequences of giving false testimony under Bosnian law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Have you also previously testified before this Tribunal in the case against Vujadin Popovic and others in July of 2007?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, in preparing to give evidence here today, did you have a chance to review your October 2005 statement to the Bosnian SIPA authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could I please have 65 ter 28941 brought up in e-court, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Pepic, while we are waiting for this document to come up on the screen, you'll see that it appears on the left side of your screen in B/C/S and it will shortly appear in English on the right side of the screen. Now -- okay. Now we have it in both languages. Could you look at the first page that's on the screen of the B/C/S, and indicate whether you recognise the signature at the bottom to be yours?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'll now ask if we could go to the last page of the document, and while we are waiting for that to come up, Mr. Pepic - yes, we have it now - I'll ask you again if you recognise the signature at the bottom in the left to be yours?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So do you recognise this document to be your statement to the SIPA authorities in October 2005?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you had a chance to review this statement. Did you have any corrections that you wished to make to this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. We'll go through those now. Can you please indicate what changes you have in mind? Can you please tell us, what's the first change you had -- that you wanted to make? If I understood you correctly there were some changes you wanted to make to the document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning, the year of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. And what is the correct year of birth?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1970, whereas here it reads "1974."

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Were there any other corrections you wanted to make?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: On page 2, if we can have it, it reads, "Execution by firing squad." I don't recall using that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you recall what word you did use?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: "Shooting," merely "shooting", from what I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we see you signed this document in multiple places. You did have a chance to review it, is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Bearing that in mind, are there any other changes that you wished to make?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Not for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, let me just attempt to assist Their Honours in locating where this is in the B/C/S, this reference you just made, both in the B/C/S and also in the English. I don't believe it's on page 2 but, Your Honours, if you'll give me a moment I'll see if I can find where it is. Now it would be on the B/C/S it is sentence straddling pages 4 and 5. In the English, Your Honours, this would be in page 9, the first paragraph which is not a full paragraph, near the bottom, four lines from the bottom, the sentence beginning in English, "I asked him." And I believe in the next line we see that phrase "executing them by fire."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to be clear, does it mean instead of saying "executing them by fire," just say "shooting them"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what it reads. "Shot them," "pucali." I don't recall using the word "streljanje."

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just for the record, the word "streljanje" does indeed appear in the statement. It would be in the B/C/S at the very top of page 5, the third word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, apart from the word being used, shooting them by fire, if you shoot at someone in such circumstances, that is shooting in order to kill them, or is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we should read that as, "I asked him what was going on now and replied -- he replied that they were firing on the Muslims," that is shooting them to kill them. That is what I understand, shoot them dead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That is an issue that I will return to in my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Pepic, before we continue I want to ask one area of clarification. Now, in your SIPA statement, you talk about the events at the Kravica warehouse. Do you recall whether those events occurred on the 12th of July or on the following day, on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall, but it's more likely to have been the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. And it's more likely. Well, if this may help your recollection, do you remember that in your testimony in the Popovic case, when you were cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic, who is in the courtroom today, do you remember telling Mr. Stojanovic that it was in fact the 13th that -- 13th of July that those events occurred? Does that assist your recollection of which day these events were?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll continue on with the foundation of the 92 ter statement then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Pepic, apart from these corrections we just discussed, if you were asked today about the same matters in the SIPA statement would you provide the same information in substance to this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just one moment. Your Honours, if I may have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just a matter of a very specific clarification. When -- Mr. Pepic, when you indicated that recalling your testimony in the Popovic case would refresh your recollection, does that mean that you are -- are you saying that it was the 13th of July that the Kravica warehouse events occurred, just to be clear?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: I'm not that sure, but it's probably the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, having taken that solemn declaration here today, do you affirm that the information in your SIPA statement is truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the dates and all that, I don't recall that all too well. Was it the 11th, the 12th, the 13th, there I'm a bit --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Pepic, let me ask my question again: You reviewed your SIPA statement. You've made some very specific corrections, very specific corrections. Now, with those corrections, is that SIPA statement, the information therein, is it truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Well, partly yes, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well, what part is not truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about the dates, as I say. Did it happen on the 12th, did it happen on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, is there any other matter where you think it would not be accurate, apart from date and apart from the use of the word we just discussed a minute ago? So leave all that aside, apart from that, is there anything else which would not be accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. The rest is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 28941 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence will object to this being tendered for the following reasons: First, it is unusual that statements given before official bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina should be admitted as evidence in conjunction with his testimony provided before the Tribunal pursuant to 92 ter, if my understanding is correct. Our suggestion is that the record of statement given to SIPA does not meet the requirements for admission into evidence pursuant to 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, does Rule 92 ter - and the same question, of course, for Mr. Shin - apply at all to this statement? This is not a statement taken for the purposes of this Tribunal. So therefore, I'm looking at both parties a little bit confused by your approach that this would be covered by Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Rule 92 ter reads: "Evidence of a witness in the form of a written statement or transcript of evidence given by a witness in proceedings before this Tribunal." That's what Rule 92 ter reads. Now, I've been working here for a while and I've seen a lot of statements given to other authorities to be admitted into evidence, not under Rule 92 ter but just under Rule - what is it, 89(C) - so I'm both puzzled by your response and I wouldn't have said anything about it, Mr. Shin, but since this is now the response, I wonder whether you think that apart from it perhaps being good to verify that the witness is still standing behind his statement, whether Rule 92 ter applies at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if I may. The Prosecution's position is that Rule 92 ter does not exclude the introduction of a statement such as the SIPA statement. We note that in the 6th of February, 2013, decision on 92 bis motion by the Prosecution that the Trial Chamber had noted that a cantonal court statement was satisfied the requirements of 92 bis in that instance, specifically referencing the caution to tell the truth and the consequences of false testimony. Otherwise, we do -- we would submit that this statement does otherwise achieve the objective of a focused presentation of the evidence and we have no other statement for this witness. We of course have the transcript and in our 92 ter motion we had tendered that in the alternative if the SIPA statement were not accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, anything to add, anything to further illustrate how Rule 92 ter would apply in relation to this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, briefly. During our preparations for this witness's testimony, we received a list from the Prosecution listing the alternatives as to the evidence that would be admitted under 92 ter. This is a highly unusual situation. We have a filing on which the Trial Chamber has not ruled yet. When we said that we are unable to prepare the way we are being asked to do, we had to prepare for both these alternatives because we did not know how the Chamber would rule in view of the Prosecution's position. The -- however, the position of the Defence is clear. We believe that this would be a precedent outside of the standards that have so far been applied in this trial. We believe that the SIPA statement would not rise up to the requirements of 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is there any objection against admission under Rule 89(C)?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have an objection regarding that, but then the transcript from the Popovic case would be under 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are at this moment focusing exclusively on the SIPA statement, Mr. Shin, for admission now, that's what you tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next step, we'll see when we come to that. Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28941 receives number P1543, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1543 is admitted. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will first hear any further submissions before we finally decide on admission. At the same time, it's time for a break. We have not made much progress in hearing the testimony of the witness yet, but I hope that that will change soon after the break. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take the break first. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. After the break, Witness, we hope to hear the substance of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Shin, when you tendered the SIPA statement, the Chamber understood that if we would admit it, that you would not tender the transcript any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, they were offered in the alternative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the decision already pronounced, that we admit the SIPA statement and we just have to -- that's P1543 now. The admission of the SIPA statement stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while we are waiting for the witness, just one thing. If I understood your decision, this SIPA statement would be under 85(C). So then there is the question of tendering the transcript, in the alternative, under 92 ter. So in that way, in our submission, in May 2013, we said why we believe this witness should be questioned viva voce and that the transcript is not suitable to be used under 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, a minute ago I asked you whether there was any objection against admission of the SIPA statement under Rule 89(C), not 85(C), and you said there was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 89(C), Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 89(C), and then you said there were no objections. Therefore, that is admitted and there was no objection to it, at least not any more in court. Mr. Shin, you may proceed and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Pepic, you may have heard this, I'm not sure, but your SIPA statement has been tendered into evidence here. Now, I'm going to ask you a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: But first, Your Honours, may I read a summary of the witness's evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And as I understand it, Mr. President, I've explained to counsel for the witness the purpose of the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is now read is not evidence but just summarises what your evidence is. Please proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In July 1995, Milenko Pepic was a member of the 2nd Sekovici Detachment of the Special Police forces brigade or Special Police Brigade commanded by Rade Cuturic also known by the nickname Oficir. His unit was sent to Srebrenica on 11th of July, 1995, and on the following day to the Potocari area. Subsequently, his unit was assigned to duty along the Bratunac to Konjevic Polje road. While there, Mr. Pepic heard Muslims being called from the woods to surrender. He could also hear detonations from the area south of the road. At one point, Mr. Cuturic told Mr. Pepic and other men that Muslim prisoners at Sandici would have to be escorted to a warehouse in Kravica. Mr. Cuturic then took Mr. Pepic to a small bridge on that road in the village of Kravica, gave him a Motorola radio and told him to stop the buses carrying Muslim women and children, when Cuturic called Mr. Pepic on the radio. When Mr. Cuturic contacted him via radio, Mr. Pepic stopped the vehicles. He then heard shooting and detonations coming from the direction of Kravica. Mr. Cuturic arrived at Mr. Pepic's position shortly after on his way to Bratunac and told Mr. Pepic about an incident in which he had been injured and said that the Muslims at the Kravica warehouse were being killed. The shooting continued. Later, Mr. Cuturic returned from the direction of Bratunac and ordered Mr. Pepic to allow the vehicles to continue. Later that day, Mr. Pepic passed the Kravica warehouse and saw piles of hay in front which he believed were now covering the bodies of the Muslim victims so that the women and children on the buses would not see them. Mr. President, that concludes my summary, and if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have any additional questions for the witness you may put them to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pepic, as you've heard, the Judges have your SIPA statement so I won't be going over in detail the information there. I'll be asking a few questions along some specific areas. Now, I'd like to begin by asking you a few questions about your unit, the 2nd Sekovici Detachment. Now, to be clear, that 2nd Sekovici Detachment, that's part of a Special Police Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You state -- in your statement you say that the commander of the Sekovici detachment was Rade Cuturic. Now, who was Mr. Cuturic's direct superior?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Rade Cuturic was the commander from mid-June, if I recall, and his superior was the brigade commander, Goran Saric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Who was Mr. Cuturic's direct superior in the area of Srebrenica on the days of July 11th, 12th and 13th?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well, do you recall telling the Judges at this Tribunal in the Popovic trial that his direct superior in the area of Srebrenica was Ljubisa Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Ljubisa Borovcanin was the deputy brigade commander, and he was in the area around Srebrenica. He was probably his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: He was probably or he was, based on your knowledge and your experience?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was the deputy commander of the special brigade superior to our detachment commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pepic. Now, you have in your statement also that there were three platoons of the 2nd Sekovici Detachment. My question for you: How many men are we talking about in these three platoons together?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. The approximate number in the platoons would be up to 30, perhaps fewer men, but I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. So that would be up to 90 approximately, in the three platoons together?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: If each of them numbered 30, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you identified in your statement the leader of the 3rd Platoon to be someone known as by the nickname Cop. What was his real name in full?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Milenko Trifunovic, aka Cop. He was the commander of the 3rd Detachment, the detachment from Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And your platoon -- I'm sorry, in the translation we have that he was commander of the 3rd Detachment. Did you mean he was commander of the 3rd Detachment or the 3rd Platoon?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you as you state were in the 2nd Platoon. During the days of 11 to 13 July, who was the commander of that platoon?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: We didn't have a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So who gave you orders?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: We received orders directly from our detachment commander, Cuturic, Oficir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pepic. I'm going to move now to another area, and it's some questions I have about the equipment that the 2nd Sekovici Detachment had with them. Now, you and members of your unit were dressed in camouflage overalls, that is in your statement. Just to be clear, by "overalls" do you mean that these were one-piece uniforms or two-piece uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Overalls mostly, "kombinezoni."

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Is a "kombinezoni," does that mean that's one-piece -- that's a one-piece uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, one piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, your detachment, what insignia or emblem did the members of your detachment wear?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: We had insignia above our left arm which said, "Special Police Brigade" with the Serbian flag in there, the double-headed eagle, and then the numbers were written out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to ask you if you could explain to these Judges what kinds of mechanised weaponry or armoured vehicles did the 2nd Sekovici Detachment have?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: We had a tank, we had a Praga, we had a three-barrelled gun, mortars, and automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, could I just seek some clarification. You said on the insignia on your left arm also contained the numbers, the numbers were written out. Numbers of what? Of the detachment or of -- could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The detachment numbers, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I believe the witness said "voda" again which may be "platoon." Was that platoon or detachment, Mr. Pepic? What number was on that patch, the platoon or detachment number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The numbers of the detachment. The 2nd Detachment had a number beginning with 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what, then, followed after the 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The rest of the numbers, 2033, 2022. My number was 2043. It went in order of issuance of the uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it was -- the start was the number of the detachment and then what followed was an individual number related to your uniform and therefore to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, did your -- did the detachment, the Sekovici detachment, did it also have mortar support?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Was that part of the three platoons or was that a separate unit within the detachment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: They were separate, within the detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you also -- in addition to automatic weapons, did you also have hand-held rockets known as zoljas?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Pepic. I'm going to move now to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, on the question about vehicles, the witness answered -- at least part of his answer was that they had a tank. Did you have any other vehicles apart from that tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had a Praga and we had --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, if we just go back to page 30, lines 15 and 16, I believe the witness testified that there was also the Praga and a three-barrelled gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Praga being exactly what?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Pepic, if you could please answer His Honour's question. Could you describe what a Praga is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but a Praga is an armoured vehicle with two cannons mounted on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you had no other vehicles apart from the tank and the Praga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had two military trucks, 110 and 150, and we also had a bus that belonged to our detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pepic, I'd like to focus briefly on your time before Mr. Cuturic took you to the small bridge in the village of Kravica, this time when you were on the road. Now, you explained in your statement that you were deployed on the road between Sandici and Kravica. And by "you" I mean your detachment. Now, while you were there, this is the same day as the events of the Kravica warehouse, but before you were posted at that bridge, did you see buses along that road carrying Muslim women and children in the direction of Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you describe in your statement that you heard detonations from the direction of the woods on the hill south of that road. Did you also hear that Praga firing during that time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: I don't recall hearing the Praga but I did hear detonations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well, would it refresh your recollection if I -- if I told you that you testified in the Popovic trial that you did hear a Praga firing?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In addition to the detonations, this may be an obvious question, did you also hear shooting from that direction?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And this shooting, can you describe what that firing sounded like to you, generally?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: There was shooting from infantry weapons, from the direction of Sandici and from the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going to move on to a slightly different area. Mr. Pepic, in your statement, you describe that Mr. Cuturic came to tell you that a group of Muslims located at Sandici needed to be escorted to the Kravica warehouse. And your statement goes on to describe some of the following events in detail, so just a few questions here. After you receive the call from Mr. Cuturic, while you were at that point on the bridge, you stop the convoy of buses carrying the Muslim women and children. And then you mentioned that at one point you heard shooting coming from the direction of the hangar. Just so that we are clear here, by hangar you're talking about the Kravica warehouse; is that -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You also describe in your statement that you heard bomb detonations that could be heard coming from the direction of the warehouse. Now, by bomb detonations, can you describe to the Judges here what types of explosions those were, as far as you could understand?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: They were loud, strong detonations. You could hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you understand what types of explosives were detonating? Could you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: I assumed they were bombs, that these were explosions from bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'll move on, then. Now, having stopped the convoy of buses, you explain in your statement that the gunfire could be heard by the drivers and the civilians on those buses. My question to you is: Do you -- do you recall how the drivers and the civilians, the women and children on those buses, how they reacted?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: I don't remember how they reacted, but shooting could be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you will recall that you described in the Popovic trial the nature of this shooting. Now, this is the shooting from the warehouse as well as the bomb detonation that you described as coming from the direction of the warehouse. You described in the Popovic trial what this sounded like, particularly in comparison to the shooting you heard earlier in the day, that earlier shooting coming from the hill south of Sandici. Can you describe now for these Judges in this Chamber what was different about the shooting coming from the Kravica warehouse, the sound or the quality of it, what was different between that compared to that earlier shooting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: It was different because it was coming only from one side, this shooting and the detonations. No shooting was heard from the side of the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And in addition, if you could try to describe for these Judges here the intensity of that shooting compared to the shooting earlier, so the intensity of the shooting you heard coming from the warehouse versus the shooting you heard coming earlier in the day from the hills?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: It was stronger. There was more fire. You could hear it more loudly than before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like, Mr. Pepic, if you could assist the Judges here in understanding exactly where your position was along the road. I'm going to ask you some questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So if I could please have 65 ter 14885 brought up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I meanwhile ask a question to clarify. You were asked about the intensity of the shooting, and your answer said -- in your answer, you said: "It was stronger. There was more fire. You could hear it more loudly than before." Now, when you said there was more fire, does that mean that you heard more shots, more firing apart from it being louder also, to be more frequent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Pepic, before we go to this document I'd like to ask you one question relating to what Mr. Cuturic told you. Now, in your statement, you described that when he told you about the prisoners at Sandici who needed -- who were going to be moved to Kravica, in your statement - and this is in English page 8, the third paragraph, and the B/C/S page 4, the 8th paragraph - you say that he -- Mr. Cuturic sneered when he said that. How did you understand that sneer? What did that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: I said that he laughed. I didn't say that he sneered, but that he said it with a smile. He was probably thinking of us so that we wouldn't get frightened. That's how I understood it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, if we could go back to -- I'm sorry, I may have thrown our court officers -- if we could please go back to 65 ter 14885.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: While we are waiting for that, Mr. Pepic, you'll recognise this as a map marked by you during your testimony in the Popovic trial in July 2007. You've made some markings and I'm just going to ask you to briefly explain those markings to the Judges of this Chamber. First of all, in the centre of this map we see Kravica, and I'd like to ask you - that blue X in that red circle, if you could take a look at your screen you see that blue X in the red circle next to the initials MP - now does that -- would it be correct that that blue X is marking where you were standing when you were posted on the bridge by Mr. Cuturic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we just go a little bit to the left, we see a small red X just to the south of that road. Would it be correct that when you marked that you meant that to be the location of the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just so that we complete the picture here, below that little red X which marks the location of the Kravica warehouse, we do see some other markings. Would it be correct that those markings are KW -- are the letters KW?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: From what I can see, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. I will move on. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you move on, what do the letters KW mean, sir? What do they signify?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be of assistance here. The witness -- we could seek his recollection by reading the portion of the Popovic transcript but to smooth the transition, the Judges had asked him to mark that to indicate what that red X was, so it may be that the languages -- the letters represent a language not known to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say you're going to assist? Are you going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I can -- I'll read -- I'll read the passage to him from the transcript, Your Honours. And this is from the transcript, from the Popovic trial. It's page 13571, lines 16 through 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Pepic, if you could just tell me if you recall this exchange? In that case, Judge Agius was asking you, "Could you now indicate --" quote: "Could you now indicate -- first let's start like this, first beneath that X could you put the letters KW. Do you -- do you recall that? Do you recall the Judge asking you to make those markings?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you recall that by that the Judge meant you to mark where the location of the Kravica warehouse, which is KW in English, where the Kravica warehouse is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I apologies to Your Honours for not being more clear about that. I can see that raised a question. With that, Your Honours, I would tender this 65 ter 14885.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 14885 receives number P1544, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1544 is admitted. Please proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Pepic, now moving a little forward in time again, you describe in your statement that after you had been instructed to permit the traffic to flow again, you describe that you had been picked up by the detachment bus and that you were on your way to Konjevic Polje and you passed the Kravica warehouse. You explain in your statement that you saw hay in front of the warehouse and that you believed that hay was there to cover the bodies of Muslims who had been killed so that the women and children in the passing convoy would not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And this is on page 9 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, I would just ask you a few questions about another document that you've seen in the Popovic trial. If I could have 65 ter 14891. Mr. Pepic, while we're waiting for this document to come up, let me just explain that it is an aerial photograph marked by you during your testimony in the Popovic trial. And again, I'll just be asking to you explain what those markings are to the Judges in this Chamber. I think we need a minute -- there it is. Now, Mr. Pepic, in the middle of this photograph, we see - let's say horizontally and parallel to the road - a building that you have marked in red ink. Would it be correct that on the top of that building are two letters, ZZ, which is the B/C/S acronym for agricultural co-operative?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And that is what you mean by the Kravica warehouse; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, on the front of this building, on the right-hand side, we see three Xs. Do you recall that those Xs that you had -- by marking those Xs what you meant to mark?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: I marked the traces that bullets left on the walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And in front of the middle of those Xs, extending a little to the right there we see what looks like an oval. Now, while -- when testifying in the Popovic trial, do you recall what you meant that oval to mean?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: I marked approximately the area where I saw that heap of hay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you recall now in your statement, and this is again page 9 English, page 5 B/C/S, that there was more hay to the right as well as the hay that you drew that circle around? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Well, it was strewn roughly the way I marked it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 65 ter 14891.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 14891 receives number P1545, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pepic, I'm going to move on to a slightly different topic and actually moving back to one of the issues we discussed earlier. You discussed in your statement when Mr. Cuturic told you something that happened at the Kravica warehouse where an individual nicknamed Krle was killed, and in this incident you describe in your statement that Mr. Cuturic told you he had grabbed -- he had responded by grabbing the barrel of the weapon that had been used. Now, first, a quick question on Krle. Krle, that's a nickname; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What was the full -- the real name of this Krle?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: His first name is Krsto. We called him Krle. I don't recall his surname. So Krsto is his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when Mr. Cuturic was telling you about these events, and this is perhaps an obvious question, but just so that we are clear, the shooting of Krle and Mr. Cuturic grabbing the barrel, how soon did the one action follow the other? Again perhaps an obvious question but, please, if you can answer as you understood this.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember. I don't remember what the interval could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: But would it have been seconds or minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't the first question whether this was told by Mr. Cuturic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that was in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Your Honour, sometimes I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but the witness of course, his answers suggested more or less that he was talking from his own observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Ah, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say, I don't know whether it was seconds or minutes, that is a bit ambiguous as to what you're telling us about, whether you're telling what someone else told you or whether you're talking from your own observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. Honour -- Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was my problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Pepic, if I could try this question again so that it's clear, as Mr. Cuturic was telling you about what happened with Krle and about what happened with grabbing the barrel, did it -- did you understand how close in time these events were? Just those two actions: The shooting of Krle, the grabbing of the barrel of the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. I don't know how fast or how slow he could have --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: But do those incidents occur one after the other, the shooting and then the grabbing of the gun? Just simply that.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly if they did. Or what the sequence of events was. They seized Krle's rifle off him, they killed him, and then how much time passed before he managed to snatch the barrel and sustain injuries in the process, I don't know how much time passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you the following: Did he say something like, he took the weapon, he snatched the weapon, started shooting, I immediately took the barrel; or did he say he tried to shoot others as well, and then I grabbed the barrel; or did he not say anything about how much time there was between the shooting of Krle and grabbing the barrel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't tell me anything about the time that passed between the shooting and him grabbing the barrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Witness, you do describe - this is be page 9 of the English page 4 of the B/C/S - that about ten minutes after hearing the radio call regarding this fatality that Mr. Cuturic came by your position. So I'll continue. Now, I'd like to show you a document which I believe you've seen before. And this is Prosecution Exhibit 1477, if we could have that up, but if I understand correctly we are not to broadcast that. Now, Mr. Pepic, while we are waiting for this to come up on the screen, perhaps I have the wrong --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just one moment, please, Your Honour. Yes, I understand I do have the correct exhibit number but not the correct document on our screen so perhaps I can try again. P01477.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Great. Thank you very much. And if we could have English up as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Pepic, if you could just look at the left-hand side there and maybe the writing is a little small but I think you can make it out, in the third row, third column, you see the name Dragicevic, the parentheses, Bogoljub, Krsto. Now, do you know -- let me just ask, is that -- does this relate to the Krle that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Dragicevic, Krsto.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Is that Krle?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Well, probably yes, Krle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we go over to the right three columns, first two columns over we see the word Skelani and to the right we see Special Police Skelani. Now, Special Police Skelani, that would refer to the Special Police Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Skelani Platoon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When you say Skelani Platoon, you're -- that's also known sometimes as the 3rd Platoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Platoon, Skelani, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now my final area of questions, I'd like to ask now you mentioned in your statement - and this is English page 9, B/C/S pages 4 and 5 - you mentioned that at that time, this would presumably be in July 1995, you did not know who was firing upon the people in the Kravica warehouse. That was, of course, back in -- a number of years ago. Have you, since then, learned who was firing on the Muslims who were at the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well, are you aware that several persons have been convicted before the state court in Bosnia for the killing at Kravica? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you've actually testified in one and possibly more of those cases; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: More than two. Three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, were any of these persons who have been convicted at the state court, were they members of the 2nd Sekovici Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. A final question here. You mention that on the night of 13th of July, when you were with your colleagues in an abandoned house near Konjevic Polje, you mention -- and this is page 10 of the English, page 5 of the B/C/S. You mention that Mr. Cuturic came by and spoke to you about the killing of the civilians at the Kravica warehouse. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In your statement you say that he told you it was "not a good thing," quote, "not a good thing." Now, my question to you is when he was telling you this, did you have the impression that -- or did you understand Mr. Cuturic to believe himself in any way responsible for these killings?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: I didn't give it any thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you -- did he say anything about who he believed was responsible for these killings?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: He didn't say anything. He only said that sooner or later, time will come when somebody will be held responsible for what has been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, with that I do have one more question. He said someone would be held responsible. When he said "somebody," do you think he meant him or any of the people who were under his command?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: It is possible that he thought as much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Shin. Is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pepic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You'll find Mr. Stojanovic to your left and Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pepic, good day to you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to tell the Chamber where you were physically present before you came out to the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Our detachment was at the Sarajevo battle front, close to a place called Srednje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you left for Srebrenica and Bratunac, were you at all familiar with the task that you were to expect?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What were all of you who were in that vehicle heading from Sarajevo to Vlasenica thinking?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: We believed that we were on our way to the base. However, on our journey we were told that we were heading to the territory of Bratunac and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point before arriving in the Bratunac area receive any specific information or order about your impending tasks?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was your first task on your arrival in the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: We were dispatched to Bjelovac. We spent a night there in an abandoned house or school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain the whereabouts of the village of Bjelovac in relation to Srebrenica and Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: The village of Bjelovac is in the municipality of Bratunac, 4 to 5 kilometres upstream the Drina in the direction of the Sase monastery.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your first specific task was on the following morning after your arrival in the Bratunac area; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You were deployed to the Potocari area. Can you tell the Chamber how did it happen that you specifically received your assignment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Our assignment was to search the terrain to the right of the Bratunac-Srebrenica road, so to the right of the road in the direction of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What time of day was it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who issued the order to you, specifically?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: We received our order from our detachment commander, Oficir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "Oficir," would it be fair to say that this is a nickname for the detachment commander, Rade Cuturic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Rade Cuturic, also known as Oficir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As you were carrying out that first order that you received, did you engage in combat with the BH Army at all?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any civilian population present in the area that you searched?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point happen to be in Potocari among the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did it take you to carry out that combat task?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. More than an hour, an hour and a half, perhaps, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you received another order?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And which order was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PEPIC
utterances.text: The order was that we should withdraw from that stretch of the terrain and head for Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
